item.title: What’s doing for Halloween
item.dc:creator: Tribeca Citizen
item.description: Time to mark calendars for the dozen Halloween events happening around the neighborhood.
item.content:encoded:
Getting a jump on the Halloween planning, since I know folks are already feeling it. As usual, neighborhood storefronts will be handing out candy on Saturday, Oct. 31, shortly after school gets out. I will update this list as events are added.

WASHINGTON MARKET PARK
12th Annual Pumpkin Carving Contest
The Friends of Washington Market Park will hold its annual Pumpkin Carving Contest on Saturday, Oct. 24, from 3 to 6p. Bring your carved pumpkin to the park between 3 and 5; judges will announce awards at 5:30.

Annual Halloween Parade & Concert
Halloween Parade on Sunday, Oct. 25, starting at 1p from Greenwich and Beach. The parade will queue up starting at approximately 12:45p and will be led by The Queer Big Apple Marching Corps! The marching band will play till 2p on the park lawn, followed by the School of Rock House Band, jamming from the park’s gazebo.

THE DISPLAY & PARTY AT 21 JAY STREET
The residents of 21 Jay put up an elaborate Halloween installation on the corner at Greenwich — and for the past few years, the building has also closed the street for a block party with an inflated corn maze and DJ. This year it’s official, and part of the city’s Trick-or-Streets program.

TRICK-OR-STREETS NEARBY
There are several other closed streets nearby set up as part of the city’s Trick-or-Streets program, including a citywide party set for Wednesday, October 28, from 3 to 7p on Canal and Orchard/Essex; an event at Barnett Newman Triangle and the Arches under the Brooklyn Bridge. See more info here.

Photo by Julienne Schaer

PUMPKIN POINT AT GOVERNORS ISLAND
Governors Island will host its free family-friendly pumpkin patch at Nolan Park on Saturday, October 24, and Sunday, October 25, from 10a to 5p. Festivities will include trick-or-treating, music and crafts, a Fall Foliage Tree Tour, fall-themed food and drink from island vendors, and more. Performances will include traditional and contemporary folk music curated by long-time Governors Island event partner Porch Stomp, daily performances by Hopalong Andrew, and puppet theater by Cara’s Caterpillars. More info here.

THE SEAPORT
Bowne & Co. will host free Halloween Paper Crafts and Letterpress Printing on October 11 from noon to 2p at 207 Water. Come for a free hands-on experience crafting Halloween paper decorations, paper chains and folded-paper bats. Pre-registration is encouraged and walkups will be accommodated. Ages 5 and up.

Halloweekend at the Seaport Museum
October 31 | 11a to 5p | Free museum admission
The tall ship Wavertree will host a Sailors’ Superstitions spooky scavenger hunt plus Halloween treats and crafts on Pier 16, and trick or treating in the neighborhood from 3 to 5p. More info here.

item.content:encoded:
JAZZ LUNCH IN BOGARDUS PLAZA
Bogardus Plaza will host an October Jazz Lunch Series every Wednesday from 12:30 to 2p. A different jazz ensemble will perform live on the plaza. See more here.

ROCK THE BLOCK WITH CHABAD
Chabad of Tribeca will host its annual Community Street Fair — Fall Edition on Sunday, October 18, from 11a to 1p, on Duane between Greenwich and Hudson. The event is free and geared towards families. There will be music and jams, a moon bounce, giant slides, animal fun, a big bubble station, a Youth Zone with soccer, basketball and chess, a toddler area with sensory play, a special Mitzvah project, ices, sweet treats and more. RSVP is required for security purposes.

AUTUMN FESTIVAL AT GOTHAM PARK
Gotham Park and Welcome to Chinatown are teaming up for a three-day Mid-Autumn Festival from Friday, October 2, through Sunday, October 4, from 1 to 7p each day at Gotham Park, 1 Rose Street beneath the Brooklyn Bridge. The festival will bring together food, art, music, cultural performances, all-ages activities, more than 20 local AAPI food and retail vendors, and an installation of more than 100 community-painted lanterns. For more information and to register, see the Eventbrite listing here.

ALSO, LONGEST TABLE AT GOTHAM PARK
Gotham Park will host a Longest Table event on Sunday, October 18, from 1 to 3p. For the free community potluck, guests are invited to bring a dish, drink or centerpiece to share, and Gotham Park will provide the tables and chairs. This year’s gathering will have a harvest theme, with neighbors encouraged to decorate their tables. For more information and to register, see the Eventbrite listing here.

item.title: A documentary honors the work of the Sanitation Department after 9/11
item.dc:creator: Tribeca Citizen
item.description: DSNY also unveiled a new memorial at the Spring Street garage just north of Canal on West Street.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Sanitation has produced a documentary titled “Beyond the Rubble, The Story of Sanitation and Recovery After 9/11,” which aims to honor the work of Sanitation employees who served at Ground Zero and Fresh Kills in fall 2001 and beyond. The film includes extensive archival footage and first-hand interviews of DSNY employees from the weeks and months following the attacks.

In addition to removing 3.2 billion pounds of debris from the World Trade Center site, Sanitation also provided fuel for all vehicles working at Ground Zero, cleaned the streets and washed away dust throughout Lower Manhattan, and even removed rotting food from abandoned buildings, office cafeterias and restaurants in the days following the attacks — all while continuing to pick up the trash every single day from every neighborhood across the five boroughs.

The department’s work at Ground Zero continued until June 7, 2002.

Much of the material removed from the site was placed onto barges and sent across the harbor to Fresh Kills. There, a forensic team that included NYPD and the FBI sifted material down to a quarter-inch mesh sieve to identify and recover more than 54,000 personal items and the remains of more than 300 victims of the attacks. DSNY’s work assisting in the largest crime scene investigation in history continued until July 26, 2002.

Five years ago, DSNY dedicated its first memorial to the employees who died of 9/11-related illnesses, with a plaque bearing their names in the lobby of the department’s headquarters at 125 Worth and Lafayette. But that initial memorial became too small to list the growing number of men and women who have died of 9/11-related illnesses. On September 11 this year, the department unveiled a new memorial on the façade of DSNY’s Spring Street garage on the highway just north of Canal.

item.title: Seen & Heard: The Great Tribeca Scavenger Hunt
item.dc:creator: Tribeca Citizen
item.description: Plus Sardi Klein photographs at Western Union; Taste of the Seaport is now on for October 24; Fidi's Lunch Box is October 7.
item.content:encoded:
THE GREAT TRIBECA SCAVENGER HUNT
Bogardus Plaza will host its Great Tribeca Scavenger Hunt on Sunday, October 18, 3 to 5p. The event is a “friendly” competition where teams race around the neighborhood finding clues, completing missions and answering trivia to win one of 11 prizes totaling over $1,800 donated by local businesses. All proceeds benefit Bogardus Plaza. Tickets are $40/person ($35 per person through 10/6) for ages 7+. Register here.

TRIBECAN SARDI KLEIN AT 60 HUDSON
Longtime Tribecan and photographer Sardi Klein will have a show of her work in the windows of the Western Union Building, aka 60 Hudson, but on the West Broadway side at the corner with Thomas. October 2 to 30. More of her work TK.

FIDI LUNCH BOX IS OCTOBER 7
The Downtown Alliance will host its annual celebration of local restaurants — Lunch Box — on Wednesday, October 7, from 11:30a to 2:30p at Fosun Plaza, 28 Liberty. The pop-up food fair features 11 restaurants including some fresh additions to the neighborhood’s dining scene. Lunch boxes are $10 each. Rain or shine. Admission is free.

TASTE OF THE SEAPORT REBOOT
The Taste of the Seaport team were forced to postpone last week’s event to Saturday, October 24, due to the high winds and rain. So there’s still time to snag tickets! More info here.

item.title: Spotlight: Greenwich St. Jewelers at 50
item.dc:creator: Tribeca Citizen
item.description: Founded in Fidi in 1976 and now on Reade, the family business is celebrating with a photo exhibition at the store on Reade Street.
item.content:encoded:
This story starts with a meet-cute at a house party in the Bronx in the early ’60s. Carl was a jeweler’s apprentice from the Bronx; Milly was a hairdresser from Williamsburg; they were both raised in Puerto Rico. He complimented her ring, which by her account was just a plastic bauble — all she could afford. They married, had two daughters and together opened a small jewelry store in the Financial District.

That was 50 years ago — 1976. Now, Greenwich St. Jewelers is run by those same daughters — Jennifer Gandia and Christine Gandia Gambale — who first forged their own path but were each drawn back to the business they grew up with.

The business, which they moved to Tribeca in 2024, is marking 50 years Downtown with a photo exhibition at the store on Reade Street titled “Adornos: Jewelry, Memory, and What We Pass Down,” open to the public in the store.

“We are native Brooklynites.” The three women live blocks apart in Bayridge. They were raised in Marine Park, but when the girls father, Carl, died, their mother. Milly, downsized and moved closer to Christina and her grandchildren. Then Jennifer downsized and moved closer to her mom.

And this is a reflection from Jennifer.

How did the business start? Go back to the beginning…
My parents came from modest backgrounds – really, they were poor. My mother was raised by a single mother and they slept four to a bed. My father’s high school had a trade program and he got into jewelry through a class they offered. He was always very artistic and creative and this was a way to carry that into a skill.

His first roles in the Diamond District were as a model maker at an engagement ring company. He carved the wax models that the molds are made from. He then moved over to a company where he did more bench work –repairs and assembly. Eventually he got his own booth on 47th Street, It’s a labyrinth over there. First you have the arcades on the street level, but then you go upstairs are there are the tiniest little offices where people do contract work and repair work. It’s its own incredible ecosystem up there.

When he and my mother started dating, she was working in a hair salon – neither went to college. They got married in ‘68 and after those first years together, they decided to open their own store.

My father was looking in the papers for a space and he saw a little ad in the New York Times that said there was a jewelry story for sale – “Call Albert,” it said, with a phone number. It was called Albert’s Jewelers at 118a Greenwich Street and he and his wife, Dorothy, ran it together. They were ready to retire and looking for someone to take it over.

That dates it right there — “Call Albert.”
Albert is now a venerated saint in our family. I think they saw something in my parents that reminded them of what they were like when they decided to open up a jewelry story. They sold it for a very very modest price. No one remembers the number now – and sometimes my mother says, “I don’t remember money ever changing hands.”

What’s so beautiful to me — it moves me to tears even now — is Albert and Dorothy stayed on with my parents for a year. They taught them the business and introduced them to all their customers. It was so generous. They became very good friends. And now there are so many Dorothy and Albert-isms — probably the number one is “You always treat your clients like they are guests in your home.” In Latino households it’s the same thing – and that was how my parents ran their business.

They didn’t have money to buy jewelry to put in the store so it was built on service. Anything my father gave my mother she would polish up and put in the window. And little by little they built a business.

How did the neighborhood change over the years they ran the store?
It’s interesting to think about what Downtown was like back then [Jennifer was born in 1974 and remembers it well]. It was predominantly mom and pop stores — small stores, independently owned. It was a real fabric of community, of people who made up the neighborhood.

What made you move to Tribeca after all those years?
That’s one of those things that Tribeca really has maintained so beautifully that most neighborhoods have lost. Maybe I still see that because I look for it. It’s hard for any neighborhood to maintain that these days because of systemically what’s happening with the economy. But here I see Balloon Saloon and Korin and Fernandez and even the new ones – like Words on Warren. The stores look different than they did 50 years ago, but they are still people who want a neighborhood where they can establish an anchor.

That’s why we moved to Tribeca – that’s such a part of our business, to provide service. I tell that to my staff all the time. That’s what’s going to keep us here. We don’t live here [Jennifer, Christina and Milly all live in separate apartments in Bayridge now, since Carl died] but that doesn’t mean we are any less committed to the neighborhood. We also don’t divide Downtown – our roots and our legacy are here, whether its Tribeca or Fidi.

How did you two join the business?
My sister and I joined in the early 2000s. We were not groomed to come into the business. Our parents were never like, “this could all be yours someday.” Our parents did not go to college – my mother was working from 12 years old – so they really wanted us to do the things they didn’t get to do. And we both did different things – I went into fashion and Christina went into finance.

My father at first said no. In their minds, their thought was go out and do what you enjoy – they perceived that you work from 9 to 5 for the man and you get the weekends off and you have a life. You are on all the time owning a business.

But I knew it was going to be really tough to survive after 9/11. They were across from an open pit for years, and while it was loyal to stay, it was very difficult. And I knew I could help them. I had been working in marketing for a few years and we agreed that I would come back for one year.

A year turned into two and then three and my sister and I started talking about all the things we could do – I’m the ideas person and my sister is the one that makes it happen. She joined us too and little by little we made it through those first five years after 9/11. We survived. By then I was at an age where my friends were getting engaged and we started to build a bridal business.

How do I put this delicately: how did the business go from such modest beginnings to the luxury retail it is now?
My mother says all the time that they never would have imagined that what they started could become what we have today. It was truly organic.

The bridal business is what really shifted the business from something so modest to where we are today. But we always maintained a core of what we are, which is a service business. Anyone can walk in with a broken chain or a remodel of an heirloom piece.

Then we started working with independent artists and really unique fine jewelry. We are really proud of that.

What’s the most satisfying part of what you do?
Internally it’s working with our team. They really deliver on the environment that our parents created – welcoming, warm. We want anyone who comes in to feel comfortable and look around. That’s very important to us because of our roots.

It’s been incredibly satisfying to anchor ourselves in a community. There was a decade where we felt really untethered. My parents always had clients who would come in and chat – they were invited to weddings and funerals and bar mitzvahs. And there was a period where that wasn’t the case because of what the area had become.

Now seeing people come in with their dogs and their kids is so rewarding and so important.

Your very favorite item right now?
I am not a favorites person — I like so much — but I love that we launched the Estate Collection. I love vintage and antique jewelry so much and so does my mother, and it’s been so fun. It’s a vibrant collection. It’s like treasure hunting.

And there’s now a younger collector who wants things from the ’80s and ’90s. For them, that’s vintage.

Where do you eat/drink/shop around here?
I really love Max – I eat from there regularly — and I am often going into Clic for gifts. If I need something beautiful I go to Stella – she wraps so beautifully.

We love Artesano and I love going to the Frenchette outpost for bread and pastries for the team. And I adore the restaurant if I can get in. And Odeon? The amount of meals I have had there over the years… and I love that you can walk in and it looks the same as it did in 1991.

I love getting flowers at Elan and even just walking into that space. We’ve done company drinks at Little More and this is a random factoid: we happen to have three women on the team who do burlesque, and they did a show at Little More. I get facials at Heyday, I buy my beauty stuff at Onda. Morgan’s makes a bangin’ bacon egg and cheese.

What does the future hold?
Now that we have settled in – it took time for us to get used to it, it’s much bigger with more staffing – we have set our sights on making more of our own jewelry. We just hired a design director to move that along.

We already have a Ceremony Collection that we started in 2019, and we will revamp and expand that. We have a collection called Chroma of colored gemstone jewelry – something we really love.

We will still work with designers but we are so close to the customer, we know we are in a great position to develop beautifully made high quality pieces that don’t have to be super expensive.

item.title: Starbucks at West Broadway and Chambers will close tomorrow
item.dc:creator: Tribeca Citizen
item.description: The coffeeshop has anchored that corner, in the base of the Cosmopolitan/Frederick Hotel, for more than two decades.
item.content:encoded:
The Starbucks on the prominent Tribeca corner of West Broadway and Chambers, in the bottom of the Frederick Hotel, will close tomorrow. There’s a sign on the door — and it tracks with the corporate announcement that the chain will close 250 stores across North America.

This one opened in 2000, according to the database Starbucks Everywhere.

The hotel told me that there are several food & bev operators already interested in the space, which, of course, is right on top of the 1/2/3. Starbucks still has an active lease there.

There are 18,000 Starbucks, so the recent closings represent just 1 percent of stores. But it also includes 99 Wall and 100 William, a reader just told me. They closed more than 600 last September, according to the AP.

But corporate said there were 60 net openings year-to-date Q3 and they have an accelerated plan to complete at least 1,500 coffeehouse “uplifts” by fiscal year-end 2026. The approximately 1% of coffeehouses that closed are locations where the company does not see a path to delivering the customer experience or long-term performance Starbucks expects.

“We have carefully reviewed our North America coffeehouse portfolio and identified locations where we do not believe we can consistently deliver the experience we want for customers and partners or where we don’t see a path to acceptable financial performance,” COO Mike Grams announced yesterday.

The resdesigns include softer seating, textures, artwork, greenery and local design touches. Below is a renovated location in Austin.

Over the past couple years, there has been a retraction of Starbucks in the neighborhood: the West Street location closed in September 2025; the location at Greenwich and Franklin closed the week before that. West Street opened in January 2024, just before the Greenwich location. In 2024 we lost two others: the one inside 32 Avenue of the Americas at Sixth and Walker, and the one on Broadway and Reade.

Back then — two and a half years ago — the company was gunning for more outlets: the goal was to add 17,000 locations by 2030 to reach 55,000 globally. (The company was founded in 1971 in Seattle, and by the time it went public in 1992, it had 165 stores. By 1996 there were a 1000 stores, including some in Japan Now there are about 36,000 stores globally, and about 350 in the city. The first one here, on 87th and Broadway, opened in 1994.)
